title: Why Does the Moon Look Huge on the Horizon? #moon
description:
It isn't bigger: a small pebble at arm's length covers the Moon high or low (about half a degree). The size change happens in your brain, and scientists still debate exactly why.

Sources
- Kaufman & Kaufman (2000), Explaining the moon illusion, PNAS 97(1), 500–505
- Kaufman & Rock (1962), The moon illusion, I, Science 136, 953–961
- Ross & Plug (2002), The Mystery of the Moon Illusion, Oxford University Press
- Wikipedia, Moon illusion

subtitles: Why does the Moon look huge on the horizon?
A small pebble at arm's length covers it, high or low.
Measured, it spans about half a degree, wherever it is.
On the horizon it's actually a little farther from you, so a touch smaller.
The difference happens in your brain.
One leading idea: we sense the sky as a flattened dome, so the horizon feels farther away than overhead.
Same size in your eye, but farther away?
So your brain blows it up.
Scientists still argue about the full answer.
But the pebble stays the same.
